title: Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files
summary: Documents the format commonly used for Comma-Separated Values files and registers the text/csv MIME type. It describes the common practice rather than defining a new standard. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4180 describes a common way to write rows of data with comma-separated fields and registers the MIME type text/csv. It also warns that CSV files vary between programs.

questions: what is the text/csv mime type
how do you escape quotes in csv
subtitle: A common CSV format description and the registered MIME type text/csv.

tldr.problem: CSV files were widely used, but implementations interpreted the format differently and IANA had no registered MIME type for CSV.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a common record and field format, gives an ABNF grammar, and registers text/csv with optional charset and header parameters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4180 records common practice rather than a single master specification. It has been updated by RFC 7111.

today: RFC 4180 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 7111. It describes common practice rather than a single master specification.

sections.title: Why CSV Needed a Description
sections.content:
Comma-separated values (CSV) files have long been used to exchange and convert data between spreadsheet programs. RFC 4180 notes that the format was common but had no formal specification, and that programs used different MIME types for CSV.

The RFC describes a format followed by many implementations and registers the MIME type text/csv. It does not claim that every existing CSV file follows one uniform specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Many programs used CSV, but they did not all follow the same written rules or use the same media type. This RFC records a common format and registers a shared name for it.

sections.title: Records, Fields, and Quoting
sections.content:
A CSV file has records on separate lines, usually separated by CRLF. A header line may appear first and should contain the same number of fields as the records. Fields are separated by commas, and spaces count as part of a field.

A field may be enclosed in double quotes. Fields containing commas, double quotes, or line breaks should be quoted. A double quote inside a quoted field is represented by two double quotes. The final record may end with a line break, but it does not have to.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record is a row, and commas separate its fields. Put a field in double quotes if it contains a comma, quote, or line break, and write an internal quote twice.

sections.title: How Quoted Fields Work
sections.content:
The RFC's grammar distinguishes escaped fields, enclosed in double quotes, from non-escaped fields. A quoted field can contain commas and line breaks without turning them into separators between fields or records.

When a quoted field contains a double quote, the quote is doubled. The RFC notes that some programs do not use double quotes, one example of the variation among existing CSV implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Quotes let a field contain characters that would otherwise split the row. A doubled quote represents one quote inside that field.

sections.title: The text/csv Media Type
sections.content:
The registered media type is text/csv. It has no required parameters. The optional charset parameter identifies the character set, and the optional header parameter says whether the first line is a header; its values are present and absent.

The RFC says CRLF denotes line breaks for this media type, while acknowledging that some implementations use other values. If an implementation does not use the header parameter, it must decide for itself whether the first line is a header.
sections.plainLanguage: The type name is text/csv. Optional parameters can identify the character set and tell a reader whether the file begins with column names.

sections.title: Differences Between CSV Implementations
sections.content:
The registration notes considerable differences among CSV implementations because there is no single master specification. Section 2 is an attempt to describe a common format, not a guarantee that every file will match it.

Implementers are advised to be conservative in what they create and liberal in what they accept. When the optional header parameter is absent, a reader must make its own decision about whether a header is present.
sections.plainLanguage: CSV files can differ from one program to another. Write files that follow the common rules, and be prepared to read reasonable variations.
